title: Rethinking Sequence Compression withTest-time Regression

paper.title: Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming.
We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation.
Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass.
This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression.
We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models.
On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin.
For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens.
These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Sequence compression is a ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures ( Qwen Team, 2026b ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) , and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into a summary vector used to score and select relevant blocks ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026a ) . In both settings, the compressor acts as a critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream. One would expect compression to be a carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling. We argue that these default compressors share a fundamental structural limitation, i.e. , they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships . Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently. As a result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted. From a statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit first-order token statistics while ignoring second-order inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive. We introduce a fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking which weighted average best summarizes a set of tokens, we let the tokens define a regression problem and take its fitted coefficients as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs a self-supervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation. This formulation creates a natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns which regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines how that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution. By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence. This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by a fixed projection or additive token combination. Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension ( i.e. , T < d T<d ), we solve the dual problem with an efficient T × T T\times T Cholesky factorization. Thus, TTR-Compressor incurs minimal overhead and introduces only 2 ​ d 2d learnable parameters per compressor, making it an effective drop-in replacement for sequence compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements on compression. In block-wise sparse attention , the compressed summary must act as a faithful retrieval key . In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors ( Hu et al., 2026 ) by a considerable margin. In visual token merging , by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve a faithful representation . Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below: • A novel compression framework. We introduce a test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem. • A practical operator. We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining. • Empirical effectiveness. As a drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Sequence compression. Compressing a sequence of tokens into a single vector is a fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Cha et al., 2024 ; Chu et al., 2024 ) to block-wise sparse attention ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms: (1) parameter-free pooling , such as mean pooling; (2) concatenation followed by learned projection ; and (3) attention-based compression , which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging ( Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . A fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations. In contrast, TTR-Compressor derives its representation as the solution to a linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above. Test-time regression and test-time training. The idea of adapting part of a network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers ( Schmidhuber, 1992 ; Schlag et al., 2021 ) and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift ( Sun et al., 2020 ) and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Behrouz et al., 2026b ; Behrouz et al., 2026a ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In-Place TTT ( Feng et al., 2026 ) further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. A parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants ( e.g. , DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025c ) , Longhorn ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , Titans ( Behrouz et al., 2026b ) ) as online regression: each layer maintains a key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet ( von Oswald et al., 2026 ) pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization. TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient, exact closed-form solution via a single T × T T\times T dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT 3 , In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and single-step approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights ( Bertinetto et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2020 ) or a fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried ( Schlag et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2025c ; Behrouz et al., 2026b ) , we use regression to directly yield a representation of a token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation ( e.g. , a visual token or a retrieval key).

sections.heading: 3 Joint Sequence Compression via Test-time Regression
sections.text: We introduce TTR-Compressor, a sequence compression operator based on test-time regression , as shown in Figure 2 (a). Given a sequence of token representations, TTR-Compressor constructs a regression problem from the tokens and uses its fitted coefficients as the compressed representation. We first present the regression formulation of compression and specify its construction, then derive an efficient solution and describe how TTR-Compressor is learned end-to-end within a model.

sections.heading: 3.1 Compression as Test-time Regression
sections.text: We formulate sequence compression as ridge regression ( Hoerl & Kennard, 1970 ) . The tokens in a sequence provide regression observations, and the fitted regression coefficients serve as a compact representation of that sequence. The regression objective encourages this representation to capture the relationships among tokens, while regularization controls the magnitude of the fitted coefficients. Given a sequence 𝑿 = [ 𝒙 1 , … , 𝒙 T ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ T × d \bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} , our goal is to compress its T T token representations into a single vector 𝒉 ∈ ℝ d \bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . We associate each token with a regression key 𝒌 t ∈ ℝ d \bm{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a scalar target v t ∈ ℝ v_{t}\in\mathbb{R} , and define the compressed representation as: 𝒉 ⋆ = arg ⁡ min 𝒉 ∈ ℝ d ​ 1 2 ​ ∑ t = 1 T ω t ​ ( 𝒌 t ⊤ ​ 𝒉 − v t ) 2 + λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝒉 ‖ 2 2 , \bm{h}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\omega_{t}\big(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{h}-v_{t}\big)^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}, (1) where ω t ≥ 0 \omega_{t}\geq 0 determines the contribution of each token and λ > 0 \lambda>0 controls regularization. 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} summarizes the sequence by fitting the key-target relationships across its tokens. The regression target v t v_{t} is meta-learned through the task loss, while the regression itself is constructed and solved for each input sequence during both training and inference. Overall, we are solving a bi-level optimization, where the outer objective is the task loss that finds the task-useful target v t v_{t} , and the inner objective is the test-time regression Eq. 1 that solves the compressed representation 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} . Here, test-time refers to fitting these input-specific coefficients; the learned model parameters remain fixed at inference. Figure 2: Overview of TTR-Compressor. (a) Bilevel learning: The inner solve formulates sequence compression as test-time ridge regression with an exact dual Cholesky solve to obtain the representation 𝒉 ∗ \bm{h}^{*} , while the regression parameters are learned end-to-end via task gradients. (b) Input-dependent second-order adaptation: By jointly coupling tokens through the Gram matrix, TTR naturally diminishes the relative influence of redundant tokens compared to additive pooling. For intuitive illustration, we set 𝑫 = 𝑰 \bm{D}=\bm{I} and uniform targets 𝒗 = 𝟏 \bm{v}=\mathbf{1} ; as typically learned in practice, a smaller regularizer 𝑫 \bm{D} further amplifies this deduplication effect, yielding an even higher relative share for distinct tokens.

sections.heading: 3.4 Fully End-to-end Training
sections.text: The target projection 𝒂 \bm{a} and diagonal parameters 𝝆 \bm{\rho} are optimized end-to-end through the differentiable closed-form solution using the original model’s training objective. Each compressor maintains its own parameters, which are shared across all input sequences. At inference time, these learned parameters remain fixed, while 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} is recomputed independently for each input sequence. TTR-Compressor therefore combines a learned regression objective with an exact, input-adaptive solution, without requiring iterative gradient-based optimization at test time.

sections.heading: 4 Understanding TTR-Compressor
sections.text: The learning process of TTR-Compressor can be decomposed into two distinct mechanisms: outer-loop training learns which regression problem is useful for compression, while the inner solution adapts the compressed representation to the current input’s statistics. We examine them separately.

sections.heading: 5 Applications and Experimental Results
sections.text: We evaluate TTR-Compressor in two settings: block-wise sparse attention for efficient language modeling, where compressed representations guide context selection, and visual token merging for efficient multimodal understanding, where they serve as the visual input to the language backbone.

sections.heading: 5.1 Block-wise Sparse Attention
sections.text: Architecture and Baselines. Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside a local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent a relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations. We adopt HiLS-Attention ( Hu et al., 2026 ) as a base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLS-Attention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only a subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references. Training and Evaluation. We train 345M-parameter language models on the FineWeb dataset ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) with an 8K context length. Training runs for 30,000 optimization steps with a global batch size of 128 sequences, corresponding to approximately 30B tokens, and uses AdamW with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} . All sparse attention variants use 64-token blocks, select up to 32 distant blocks per query, and retain a 512-token local window. Evaluation covers two complementary aspects. First, since queries use the compressed representations to retrieve relevant blocks, retrieval accuracy directly reflects compression quality. Following ( Hatamizadeh et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate on the single-needle (S-NIAH) and multi-key (MK-NIAH) retrieval tasks from RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , which require locating relevant information among distractors, as the most direct and demanding test of the compressor. We evaluate at 4K–32K context lengths, including extrapolation beyond the 8K training length. Additionally, LAMBADA accuracy and the zero-shot benchmarks in Table 2 assess contextual prediction, commonsense reasoning, and question answering. sections.heading: 5.2 Visual Token Merger
sections.text: Architecture and Baselines. High-resolution images produce many visual tokens, making their direct processing by a language backbone expensive. Modern multimodal models therefore commonly use a spatial merger to reduce the visual sequence length. A widely adopted design concatenates each 2 × 2 2\times 2 group of neighboring visual features and maps it to one token through a two-layer MLP ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ; Team et al., 2026b ) . Longer multimodal contexts and agentic workflows with repeated visual observations further motivate stronger compression, such as 3 × 3 3\times 3 merging ( Team et al., 2026a ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . We compare TTR-Compressor with the standard MLP merger. TTR-Compressor fits one regression per spatial group to compress its four or nine visual features into a single vector, which a two-layer MLP then projects to the language model’s hidden dimension. Its convolutional variant applies a 3 × 3 3\times 3 depthwise convolution to the feature map before constructing the regression targets. Training and Evaluation. We use the ViT of Qwen3-VL ( Bai et al., 2025 ) as the vision encoder and Qwen3-4B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025a ) as the language model. Training consists of two stages. The first stage trains only the merger modules on LLaVA-558K ( Liu et al., 2024a ) for one epoch with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . The second stage jointly trains the merger modules and language backbone on 1.3M instruction samples mixing image ( Liu et al., 2024b ) , multi-image ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and video ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) data for one epoch with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} . We evaluate on 4 types of benchmarks: general visual question answering (MMBench ( Liu et al., 2024c ) , MMStar ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , RealWorldQA ( xAI, 2024 ) ), knowledge-intensive multimodal reasoning (MMMU ( Yue et al., 2024 ) , AI2D ( Kembhavi et al., 2016 ) ), text, infographic, and chart understanding (OCRBench ( Liu et al., 2024d ) , InfoVQA ( Tito et al., 2021 ) , ChartQA ( Masry et al., 2022 ) ), and spatial reasoning (MMSI ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , ERQA ( Team et al., 2025 ) ). The MLP merger concatenates the features in each group and maps them with fixed weights, so the mixing does not depend on how the features relate to each other. When most features in a group are redundant, such as background patches, they dominate the merged token and wash out fine-grained details. In contrast, TTR-Compressor fits correlated features jointly and reduces the influence of redundant ones, so the merged token keeps the distinctive content within the group.

sections.heading: 6 Concluding Remarks
sections.text: In this work, we revisit sequence compression, a pervasive yet often overlooked bottleneck in modern architectures, through the lens of test-time regression. Instead of relying on fixed pooling or learned projections, we formulate token compression as an instance-adaptive ridge regression problem, allowing the compressed representation to be solved directly from each input sequence. By exploiting inter-token correlations through second-order interactions, TTR-Compressor offers a more expressive way to preserve sequence information while remaining lightweight and parameter-efficient. Its dual-form solution further makes this formulation scalable in practice. Empirically, TTR-Compressor performs strongly across both block-wise sparse attention and multimodal token reduction, improving long-context retrieval while matching standard visual mergers with significantly fewer tokens. More broadly, our results suggest that sequence compression need not be viewed as static aggregation, but as an input-dependent inference problem that adapts to the structure of each sequence. We expect this perspective establishes test-time regression as a simple, expressive, and scalable primitive for efficient foundation models.

sections.heading: Appendix C Implementation Details
sections.text: Numerical Precision. Convolution and target projection use the input precision (BF16), while regression keys and targets are cast to FP32 before the dual solve. Diagonal regularization is evaluated in FP32. We solve the positive-definite dual system using Cholesky factorization without explicitly forming an inverse, and cast the compressed representation back to the input dtype. Local Target Construction. Only the regression targets incorporate convolutional context; keys are computed from the original inputs. For language, we apply a non-causal depthwise 1D convolution with kernel size 5 5 , independently within each compression block, using two-sided zero padding of width 2 2 . The convolution has neither bias nor activation and is initialized to the identity. For vision, we use a 3 × 3 3\times 3 depthwise convolution. Each channel has its own spatial kernel, with no cross-channel mixing before the scalar target projection. The base compressor has 2 ​ d 2d effective trainable parameters: d d for the target projection and d d for diagonal regularization. A bias-free depthwise convolution with s s kernel elements adds s ​ d sd parameters and 𝒪 ⁡ ( s ​ T ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(sTd) computation. Thus, the language and vision variants require 7 ​ d 7d and 11 ​ d 11d parameters, respectively. Their total computational complexity remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}d) for fixed kernel sizes and T ≪ d T\ll d .

sections.heading: Appendix D Experimental Details
sections.text: Block-wise Sparse Attention. HiLS-Attention ( Hu et al., 2026 ) argues that small models provide a more diagnostic setting for RULER’s predominantly “find-and-copy” tasks, as larger models may compensate for retrieval inaccuracies through greater information bandwidth. We therefore follow their setup and use 345M-parameter models to evaluate compression quality. All models use 16 Transformer layers, a hidden dimension of 1,024, an FFN dimension of 4,096, and grouped-query attention with 16 query heads and 2 key–value heads. We use rank-64 query calibration. Training uses AdamW weight decay of 0.01 0.01 and gradient clipping at a norm of 1.0 1.0 ; normalization parameters, biases, and embeddings are excluded from weight decay. The learning rate warms up over the first 0.7 % 0.7\% of training and remains constant thereafter. Visual Token Merger. We use BF16 training with DeepSpeed ZeRO-1, gradient checkpointing, and a maximum sequence length of 16,384 tokens. The two stages use per-device batch sizes of 4 and 1, with gradient accumulation over 4 and 8 steps, respectively. Both stages apply a 3 % 3\% learning-rate warmup followed by cosine decay, with minimum learning rates of 10 − 5 10^{-5} and 0 0 and weight decay of 0.01 0.01 and 0.02 0.02 , respectively. For TTR-Compressor, the regression systems are solved in FP32.

sections.heading: E.1 Scaling Up Model Size and Training Budget
sections.text: To further verify that the advantage of TTR-Compressor is not merely an artifact of the smaller-scale setting used in the main paper, we scale up both the model size and the training budget. Specifically, we train a 1B-parameter model on 100B tokens and evaluate it on the same RULER subtasks across context lengths ranging from 4K to 32K. For comparison, we also scale up Attention-Weighted Pooling—the strongest baseline among all compression methods evaluated in the main paper’s 345M-parameter experiments—to the same 1B-parameter, 100B-token setting. As shown in Table 7 , TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the Attention-Weighted Pooling baseline across almost all context lengths and subtasks, achieving an average accuracy of 0.7996 compared to 0.735. Notably, the performance gap widens as the context length increases, indicating that TTR-Compressor scales more gracefully to longer contexts even when both model size and training budget are substantially increased relative to the main paper’s 345M-parameter setting. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.31574v1 [cs.LG] 22 Oct 2026 Rethinking Sequence Compression with Test-time Regression Sihan Yang Jie Huang Hanxuan Li Yifan Guo Weigao Sun Yiran Zhong Weiyang Liu The Chinese University of Hong Kong Independent Researcher Token Foundry Alibaba Group * Corresponding author spherelab.ai/ttr-compressor Abstract Sequence compression is a fundamental operation and a critical information bottleneck in efficient language and multimodal models, and yet prevailing approaches based on pooling or learned projections remain underperforming. We revisit sequence compression through the lens of test-time regression: input tokens define a regression problem whose fitted coefficients form the compressed representation. Importantly, the regression problem is learned end-to-end via backpropagation, while its coefficients are computed efficiently in closed form during the forward pass. This leads to TTR-Compressor, a general alternative to conventional pooling and projection-based compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor as the compressor for block-wise sparse attention and the visual token merger for multimodal large language models. On block-wise sparse attention, TTR-Compressor improves RULER performance over attention-based compressors by a large margin. For visual token merging, it consistently outperforms the standard MLP merger and matches its performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. These results establish test-time regression as an effective primitive for sequence compression in efficient language and multimodal models. Figure 1: Overview of TTR-Compressor. (a) Unlike pooling and projection, which process tokens independently, TTR-Compressor fits all tokens jointly and thereby captures the interplay among them. (b) TTR-Compressor outperforms existing methods on both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging. 1 Introduction Sequence compression is a ubiquitous operation in modern efficient large model architectures ( Qwen Team, 2026b ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) , and yet remains surprisingly underexplored. For example, block-wise sparse attention compresses each token block into a summary vector used to score and select relevant blocks ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ) , while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) merge neighboring visual features into compact tokens before feeding them into the language backbone ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026a ) . In both settings, the compressor acts as a critical information bottleneck. Once information is discarded, it cannot be recovered downstream. One would expect compression to be a carefully designed architectural component. However, most models rely on simple mechanisms, such as parameter-free pooling, learned projections over concatenated tokens, or at best, attention-weighted pooling. We argue that these default compressors share a fundamental structural limitation, i.e. , they aggregate tokens using weights that do not account for inter-token relationships . Mean pooling uses uniform weights, linear projection uses fixed position-dependent weights, and attention-weighted pooling scores each token independently. As a result, redundant tokens can reinforce one another, while distinctive information is diluted. From a statistical perspective, these methods primarily exploit first-order token statistics while ignoring second-order inter-token correlations, the very structure that reveals which information is redundant and which is distinctive. We introduce a fundamentally different compression strategy. Rather than asking which weighted average best summarizes a set of tokens, we let the tokens define a regression problem and take its fitted coefficients as the summary. Specifically, our proposed TTR-Compressor, constructs a self-supervised ridge-regression problem directly from the input tokens, requiring no external labels, and uses its closed-form solution as the compressed representation. This formulation creates a natural division: the outer training loop meta-learns which regression problem produces task-useful representations, while the inner closed-form solution determines how that problem should be fitted to each input. The key distinction from conventional pooling and projection arises from the Gram matrix in the regression solution. By explicitly capturing inter-token correlations, TTR-Compressor fits correlated tokens jointly, so redundant evidence has diminishing rather than purely additive influence. This input-adaptive behavior cannot be reproduced by a fixed projection or additive token combination. Moreover, learning the regularizer removes the need for ridge hyperparameter tuning in large-scale pretraining. Because the compression window is typically smaller than the channel dimension ( i.e. , T < d T<d ), we solve the dual problem with an efficient T × T T\times T Cholesky factorization. Thus, TTR-Compressor incurs minimal overhead and introduces only 2 ​ d 2d learnable parameters per compressor, making it an effective drop-in replacement for sequence compression. We evaluate TTR-Compressor on two applications that impose fundamentally different requirements on compression. In block-wise sparse attention , the compressed summary must act as a faithful retrieval key . In this setting, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms traditional baselines on RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) retrieval tasks, surpassing sophisticated attention-based compressors ( Hu et al., 2026 ) by a considerable margin. In visual token merging , by contrast, the compressed summary must preserve a faithful representation . Here, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms the widely used MLP merger across diverse compression ratios, and achieves comparable performance with 55.6% fewer visual tokens. Our contributions are summarized below: • A novel compression framework. We introduce a test-time regression framework for sequence compression, reframing token summarization as an instance-adaptive optimization problem. • A practical operator. We derive an efficient dual closed-form solution and eliminate hyperparameter tuning, making TTR-Compressor fully practical and scalable for large-scale pretraining. • Empirical effectiveness. As a drop-in component in large models, TTR-Compressor consistently outperforms conventional baselines in both block-wise sparse attention and visual token merging. 2 Related Work Sequence compression. Compressing a sequence of tokens into a single vector is a fundamental operation across modern architectures, with applications ranging from multimodal token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Cha et al., 2024 ; Chu et al., 2024 ) to block-wise sparse attention ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) . Existing compression operators largely fall into three paradigms: (1) parameter-free pooling , such as mean pooling; (2) concatenation followed by learned projection ; and (3) attention-based compression , which summarizes tokens via attention-weighted averaging ( Mohtashami & Jaggi, 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . A fundamental limitation of these families is that they compute token combinations without explicitly accounting for the inter-token correlations. In contrast, TTR-Compressor derives its representation as the solution to a linear system whose Gram matrix directly encodes these correlations, providing an expressive, drop-in replacement for the operators above. Test-time regression and test-time training. The idea of adapting part of a network on each input at inference time dates back to fast-weight programmers ( Schmidhuber, 1992 ; Schlag et al., 2021 ) and was revived as test-time training (TTT), first for robustness under distribution shift ( Sun et al., 2020 ) and then as sequence-modeling layers whose hidden states are small models updated by gradient descent on a self-supervised loss ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Behrouz et al., 2026b ; Behrouz et al., 2026a ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In-Place TTT ( Feng et al., 2026 ) further extends this paradigm by directly adapting the existing MLP projection weights of pretrained Transformers. A parallel line of work reinterprets linear attention and its descendants ( e.g. , DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025c ) , Longhorn ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , Titans ( Behrouz et al., 2026b ) ) as online regression: each layer maintains a key-to-value regressor that is refined with one gradient or delta-rule step per token and read out by the query. MesaNet ( von Oswald et al., 2026 ) pushes the inner optimization to convergence, solving the problem at every time step with conjugate gradients, while LaCT ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) updates fast weights over large, unordered chunks to improve hardware utilization. TTR-Compressor differs from these methods in two fundamental ways. First, because compression operates independently on small, disjoint blocks without cross-block dependencies, the regression admits an efficient, exact closed-form solution via a single T × T T\times T dual solve. This avoids both iterative gradient-based inner optimization (as in TTT, ViT 3 , In-Place TTT, and MesaNet) and single-step approximations (such as delta-rule updates). Second, rather than using test-time regression to produce input-dependent model weights ( Bertinetto et al., 2018 ; Sun et al., 2020 ) or a fast-weight memory that is subsequently queried ( Schlag et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2025c ; Behrouz et al., 2026b ) , we use regression to directly yield a representation of a token block. Specifically, the fitted coefficients themselves serve as the compressed representation ( e.g. , a visual token or a retrieval key). 3 Joint Sequence Compression via Test-time Regression We introduce TTR-Compressor, a sequence compression operator based on test-time regression , as shown in Figure 2 (a). Given a sequence of token representations, TTR-Compressor constructs a regression problem from the tokens and uses its fitted coefficients as the compressed representation. We first present the regression formulation of compression and specify its construction, then derive an efficient solution and describe how TTR-Compressor is learned end-to-end within a model. 3.1 Compression as Test-time Regression We formulate sequence compression as ridge regression ( Hoerl & Kennard, 1970 ) . The tokens in a sequence provide regression observations, and the fitted regression coefficients serve as a compact representation of that sequence. The regression objective encourages this representation to capture the relationships among tokens, while regularization controls the magnitude of the fitted coefficients. Given a sequence 𝑿 = [ 𝒙 1 , … , 𝒙 T ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ T × d \bm{X}=[\bm{x}_{1},\ldots,\bm{x}_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} , our goal is to compress its T T token representations into a single vector 𝒉 ∈ ℝ d \bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . We associate each token with a regression key 𝒌 t ∈ ℝ d \bm{k}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a scalar target v t ∈ ℝ v_{t}\in\mathbb{R} , and define the compressed representation as: 𝒉 ⋆ = arg ⁡ min 𝒉 ∈ ℝ d ​ 1 2 ​ ∑ t = 1 T ω t ​ ( 𝒌 t ⊤ ​ 𝒉 − v t ) 2 + λ 2 ​ ‖ 𝒉 ‖ 2 2 , \bm{h}^{\star}=\arg\min_{\bm{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\omega_{t}\big(\bm{k}_{t}^{\top}\bm{h}-v_{t}\big)^{2}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\bm{h}\|_{2}^{2}, (1) where ω t ≥ 0 \omega_{t}\geq 0 determines the contribution of each token and λ > 0 \lambda>0 controls regularization. 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} summarizes the sequence by fitting the key-target relationships across its tokens. The regression target v t v_{t} is meta-learned through the task loss, while the regression itself is constructed and solved for each input sequence during both training and inference. Overall, we are solving a bi-level optimization, where the outer objective is the task loss that finds the task-useful target v t v_{t} , and the inner objective is the test-time regression Eq. 1 that solves the compressed representation 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} . Here, test-time refers to fitting these input-specific coefficients; the learned model parameters remain fixed at inference. Figure 2: Overview of TTR-Compressor. (a) Bilevel learning: The inner solve formulates sequence compression as test-time ridge regression with an exact dual Cholesky solve to obtain the representation 𝒉 ∗ \bm{h}^{*} , while the regression parameters are learned end-to-end via task gradients. (b) Input-dependent second-order adaptation: By jointly coupling tokens through the Gram matrix, TTR naturally diminishes the relative influence of redundant tokens compared to additive pooling. For intuitive illustration, we set 𝑫 = 𝑰 \bm{D}=\bm{I} and uniform targets 𝒗 = 𝟏 \bm{v}=\mathbf{1} ; as typically learned in practice, a smaller regularizer 𝑫 \bm{D} further amplifies this deduplication effect, yielding an even higher relative share for distinct tokens. 3.2 Constructing the Regression Problem Keys and Targets. We construct regression keys by normalizing the input features and generate scalar targets using a learned projection: 𝒌 t = 𝒙 t ‖ 𝒙 t ‖ 2 , v t = 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝒙 t , \bm{k}_{t}=\frac{\bm{x}_{t}}{\|\bm{x}_{t}\|_{2}},v_{t}=\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t}, where 𝒂 ∈ ℝ d \bm{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is shared across tokens and sequences within a compressor. Key normalization ensures that 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 \bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K} measures directional (semantic) similarity alone ( Liu et al., 2017 ) . Crucially, this normalization is asymmetric, as targets retain original token magnitudes ( v t = 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝒙 t v_{t}=\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t} ). If targets were also normalized ( v t = 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝒌 t v_{t}=\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{k}_{t} ), the fitting term would reduce to 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝑲 ⁡ ( 𝒉 − 𝒂 ) ‖ 2 2 \frac{1}{2}\|\bm{K}(\bm{h}-\bm{a})\|_{2}^{2} , trivially collapsing 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} toward the sequence-invariant static vector 𝒂 \bm{a} . By preserving token norms in the targets, no constant vector can fit varying magnitudes, forcing 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} to dynamically integrate both token semantics and their relative importance. The targets are derived entirely from the input, so fitting 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} requires no additional labels. Optionally, targets can be further enriched by first applying a local convolution (1D for language and 2D for vision) to aggregate neighboring context before the projection, i.e. , v t = 𝒂 ⊤ ​ Conv ⁡ ( 𝑿 ) v_{t}=\bm{a}^{\top}\operatorname{Conv}(\bm{X}) , where Conv ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{Conv}(\cdot) denotes the convolution operator and 𝑿 \bm{X} represents the local context window of n n neighboring tokens around position t t . Alternative parameterizations of v t v_{t} are explored in the Appendix E.2 . Uniform Token Contributions. We use uniform weights ω t = 1 \omega_{t}=1 , assigning the same coefficient to every token’s regression error. Let 𝑲 = [ 𝒌 1 , … , 𝒌 T ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ T × d \bm{K}=[\bm{k}_{1},\ldots,\bm{k}_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d} and 𝒗 = [ v 1 , … , v T ] ⊤ ∈ ℝ T \bm{v}=[v_{1},\ldots,v_{T}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T} . Setting the gradient of Eq. 1 to zero gives us a closed-form solution: ( 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 + λ ​ 𝑰 d ) ​ 𝒉 ⋆ = 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 , 𝒉 ⋆ = ( 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 + λ ​ 𝑰 d ) − 1 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 . (\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K}+\lambda\bm{I}_{d})\bm{h}^{\star}=\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{v},\qquad\bm{h}^{\star}=(\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K}+\lambda\bm{I}_{d})^{-1}\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{v}. (2) Since λ > 0 \lambda>0 , the objective is strictly convex and has a unique solution. The solution combines the key-target statistic 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 \bm{K}^{\top}\bm{v} with the sequence-dependent feature geometry 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 \bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K} . Learnable Diagonal Regularization. In conventional ridge regression, λ \lambda is a tunable hyperparameter. Such tuning is expensive during large-model pretraining and complicates scaling to different model sizes. To avoid this, we replace λ ​ 𝑰 d \lambda\bm{I}_{d} with a learnable positive diagonal matrix (meta-learned via the task loss), yielding a generalized ridge regression objective ( Tikhonov & Arsenin, 1977 ) : 𝑫 = diag ⁡ ( δ 1 , … , δ d ) , δ j = softplus ⁡ ( ρ j ) , \bm{D}=\operatorname{diag}(\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{d}),\qquad\delta_{j}=\operatorname{softplus}(\rho_{j}), (3) where 𝝆 ∈ ℝ d \bm{\rho}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is trainable. The resulting objective and its solution are: 𝒉 ⋆ \displaystyle\bm{h}^{\star} = arg ⁡ min 𝒉 ​ 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝑲 ​ 𝒉 − 𝒗 ‖ 2 2 + 1 2 ​ 𝒉 ⊤ ​ 𝑫 ​ 𝒉 , \displaystyle=\arg\min_{\bm{h}}\frac{1}{2}\|\bm{K}\bm{h}-\bm{v}\|_{2}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\bm{h}^{\top}\bm{D}\bm{h}, (4) = ( 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 + 𝑫 ) − 1 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 , \displaystyle=(\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K}+\bm{D})^{-1}\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{v}, (5) which solves a regularized linear system that takes the pairwise interaction of tokens into account. 3.3 Efficient Dual-form Solution Directly evaluating Eq. 2 requires solving a d × d d\times d linear system. When the number of tokens being compressed is typically smaller than the feature dimension, we instead use the equivalent dual form ( Saunders et al., 1998 ) in order to improve the computational efficiency: 𝒉 ⋆ = 𝑲 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑲 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ + λ ​ 𝑰 T ) − 1 ​ 𝒗 . \bm{h}^{\star}=\bm{K}^{\top}(\bm{K}\bm{K}^{\top}+\lambda\bm{I}_{T})^{-1}\bm{v}. (6) This replaces the feature-space system with a T × T T\times T token-space system. Its entries depend on pairwise similarities between regression keys, allowing the fitted representation to account for correlations among tokens. We evaluate Eq. 6 by solving ( 𝑲 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ + λ ​ 𝑰 T ) ​ 𝜶 = 𝒗 (\bm{K}\bm{K}^{\top}+\lambda\bm{I}_{T})\bm{\alpha}=\bm{v} and computing 𝒉 ⋆ = 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝜶 \bm{h}^{\star}=\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{\alpha} , without explicitly forming an inverse. The resulting computational cost is 𝒪 ⁡ ( T 2 ​ d + T 3 ) \mathcal{O}(T^{2}d+T^{3}) , compared with 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d 2 + d 3 ) \mathcal{O}(Td^{2}+d^{3}) for the direct primal formulation. The dual form is therefore particularly suitable for compressing short sequences of high-dimensional features. Obtaining an Efficient Dual Solution. With the learnable diagonal regularization introduced in Section 3.2 , λ ​ 𝑰 d \lambda\bm{I}_{d} is replaced by 𝑫 \bm{D} . To obtain an efficient dual solution, we rescale the keys as 𝑲 ~ = 𝑲 𝑫 − 1 / 2 \widetilde{\bm{K}}=\bm{K}\bm{D}^{-1/2} , yielding the final form of TTR-Compressor: TTR ( 𝑿 ) = 𝑫 − 1 / 2 𝑲 ~ ⊤ ( 𝑰 T + 𝑲 ~ 𝑲 ~ ⊤ ) − 1 𝒗 \boxed{\operatorname{TTR}(\bm{X})=\bm{D}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{K}}^{\top}\big(\bm{I}_{T}+\widetilde{\bm{K}}\widetilde{\bm{K}}^{\top}\big)^{-1}\bm{v}} (7) Because 𝑫 \bm{D} is diagonal, rescaling the keys costs only 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ​ d ) \mathcal{O}(Td) , preserving the dual formulation’s overall complexity. In practice, we compute a Cholesky factorization 𝑳 ​ 𝑳 ⊤ = 𝑰 T + 𝑲 ~ ​ 𝑲 ~ ⊤ \bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}=\bm{I}_{T}+\widetilde{\bm{K}}\widetilde{\bm{K}}^{\top} , solve 𝑳 ​ 𝑳 ⊤ ​ 𝜶 = 𝒗 \bm{L}\bm{L}^{\top}\bm{\alpha}=\bm{v} through triangular solutions, and return 𝑫 − 1 / 2 𝑲 ~ ⊤ 𝜶 \bm{D}^{-1/2}\widetilde{\bm{K}}^{\top}\bm{\alpha} . 3.4 Fully End-to-end Training The target projection 𝒂 \bm{a} and diagonal parameters 𝝆 \bm{\rho} are optimized end-to-end through the differentiable closed-form solution using the original model’s training objective. Each compressor maintains its own parameters, which are shared across all input sequences. At inference time, these learned parameters remain fixed, while 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} is recomputed independently for each input sequence. TTR-Compressor therefore combines a learned regression objective with an exact, input-adaptive solution, without requiring iterative gradient-based optimization at test time. 4 Understanding TTR-Compressor The learning process of TTR-Compressor can be decomposed into two distinct mechanisms: outer-loop training learns which regression problem is useful for compression, while the inner solution adapts the compressed representation to the current input’s statistics. We examine them separately. 4.1 Task-Supervised Learning of the Compression Objective The regression objective is not prescribed independently of the task. Its targets v t = 𝒂 ⊤ ​ 𝒙 t v_{t}=\bm{a}^{\top}\bm{x}_{t} and regularization matrix 𝑫 \bm{D} are learned through the downstream use of the compressed representation. Writing 𝒉 𝒂 , 𝝆 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star}_{\bm{a},\bm{\rho}} for the regression solution, the training objective takes the form: min θ , 𝒂 , 𝝆 ⁡ 𝔼 ( x , y ) ​ [ ℒ task ​ ( F θ ​ ( 𝒉 𝒂 , 𝝆 ⋆ ​ ( 𝑿 θ ​ ( x ) ) ) , y ) ] , \min_{\theta,\bm{a},\bm{\rho}}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}\left(F_{\theta}\!\left(\bm{h}^{\star}_{\bm{a},\bm{\rho}}(\bm{X}_{\theta}(x))\right),y\right)\right], (8) where 𝑿 θ \bm{X}_{\theta} produces the input representations and F θ F_{\theta} denotes the subsequent computation. Thus, the outer objective evaluates the usefulness of 𝒉 ⋆ \bm{h}^{\star} for the final task, rather than leveraging its learnability to merely minimize the inner regression error. Learning the Targets and Regularization. This coupling can be seen directly from the gradients. Let 𝑨 = 𝑲 ⊤ ​ 𝑲 + 𝑫 \bm{A}=\bm{K}^{\top}\bm{K}+\bm{D} , 𝒈 = ∇ 𝒉 ⋆ ℒ task \bm{g}=\nabla_{\bm{h}^{\star}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}} , and 𝒔 = 𝑨 − 1 ​ 𝒈 \bm{s}=\bm{A}^{-1}\bm{g} . Differentiating the regression solution gives: ∇ 𝒂 ℒ task = 𝑿 ⊤ 𝑲 𝒔 , ∇ 𝝆 ℒ task = − sigmoid ( 𝝆 ) ⊙ 𝒉 ⋆ ⊙ 𝒔 , \nabla_{\bm{a}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{K}\bm{s},\qquad\nabla_{\bm{\rho}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{task}}=-\operatorname{sigmoid}(\bm{\rho})\odot\bm{h}^{\star}\odot\bm{s}, (9) where ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The downstream gradient therefore shapes both the scalar targets derived from tokens via 𝒂 \bm{a} and the coordinate-wise penalties imposed through 𝝆 \bm{\rho} . Consequently, the scalar targets require no predefined semantics; instead, they serve as learned measurements whose fitted coefficients yield informative representations for downstream layers. In this sense, the regression provides a structural inductive bias for compression, while outer-loop optimization steers this structural bias towards better handling the downstream task. 4.2 Input-Dependent Second-Order Adaptation Beyond learning the regression objective, the inner solve adapts the compressed representation to the correlation structure of each input. For isotropic regularization, the dual-form solution is 𝒉 ⋆ = 𝑲 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑲 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ + λ ​ 𝑰 ) − 1 ​ 𝒗 . \bm{h}^{\star}=\bm{K}^{\top}(\bm{K}\bm{K}^{\top}+\lambda\bm{I})^{-1}\bm{v}. (10) Let 𝑮 = 𝑲 ​ 𝑲 ⊤ ∈ ℝ T × T . \bm{G}=\bm{K}\bm{K}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}. Block-wise sparse attention partitions the context into blocks, scores their compressed representations against each query, and attends to tokens in selected blocks alongside a local window. The compressor therefore determines which distant information remains accessible: an uninformative summary can prevent a relevant block from being selected, regardless of the quality of its individual token representations. We adopt HiLS-Attention ( Hu et al., 2026 ) as a base framework and vary only the compressor. HiLS-Attention has three effective architectural components: hierarchical softmax attention, which combines within-block attention with learned block-level weights; low-rank query calibration, which adapts queries for scoring compressed representations; and HoPE, which applies RoPE to only a subset of feature dimensions to support length extrapolation. We compare four compressors: mean pooling, concat & projection, the attention-weighted pooling used in the original HiLS-Attention, and TTR-Compressor. Full attention and sliding-window attention serve as additional references. Training and Evaluation. We train 345M-parameter language models on the FineWeb dataset ( Penedo et al., 2024 ) with an 8K context length. Training runs for 30,000 optimization steps with a global batch size of 128 sequences, corresponding to approximately 30B tokens, and uses AdamW with a learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} . All sparse attention variants use 64-token blocks, select up to 32 distant blocks per query, and retain a 512-token local window. Evaluation covers two complementary aspects. First, since queries use the compressed representations to retrieve relevant blocks, retrieval accuracy directly reflects compression quality. Following ( Hatamizadeh et al., 2026 ) , we evaluate on the single-needle (S-NIAH) and multi-key (MK-NIAH) retrieval tasks from RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , which require locating relevant information among distractors, as the most direct and demanding test of the compressor. We evaluate at 4K–32K context lengths, including extrapolation beyond the 8K training length. Additionally, LAMBADA accuracy and the zero-shot benchmarks in Table 2 assess contextual prediction, commonsense reasoning, and question answering. High-resolution images produce many visual tokens, making their direct processing by a language backbone expensive. Modern multimodal models therefore commonly use a spatial merger to reduce the visual sequence length. A widely adopted design concatenates each 2 × 2 2\times 2 group of neighboring visual features and maps it to one token through a two-layer MLP ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ; Team et al., 2026b ) . Longer multimodal contexts and agentic workflows with repeated visual observations further motivate stronger compression, such as 3 × 3 3\times 3 merging ( Team et al., 2026a ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . We compare TTR-Compressor with the standard MLP merger. TTR-Compressor fits one regression per spatial group to compress its four or nine visual features into a single vector, which a two-layer MLP then projects to the language model’s hidden dimension. Its convolutional variant applies a 3 × 3 3\times 3 depthwise convolution to the feature map before constructing the regression targets. Training and Evaluation. We use the ViT of Qwen3-VL ( Bai et al., 2025 ) as the vision encoder and Qwen3-4B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2025a ) as the language model. Training consists of two stages. The first stage trains only the merger modules on LLaVA-558K ( Liu et al., 2024a ) for one epoch with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . The second stage jointly trains the merger modules and language backbone on 1.3M instruction samples mixing image ( Liu et al., 2024b ) , multi-image ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and video ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) data for one epoch with a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} . We evaluate on 4 types of benchmarks: general visual question answering (MMBench ( Liu et al., 2024c ) , MMStar ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , RealWorldQA ( xAI, 2024 ) ), knowledge-intensive multimodal reasoning (MMMU ( Yue et al., 2024 ) , AI2D ( Kembhavi et al., 2016 ) ), text, infographic, and chart understanding (OCRBench ( Liu et al., 2024d ) , InfoVQA ( Tito et al., 2021 ) , ChartQA ( Masry et al., 2022 ) ), and spatial reasoning (MMSI ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , ERQA ( Team et al., 2025 ) ).
